content_voiceover: Treatment of Burkitt lymphoma is risk-adapted, and the single most important point for boards is this: CHOP is not adequate therapy, it under-treats this highly proliferative disease. Risk stratification starts with low risk, defined as normal LDH plus stage one disease with a single extra-abdominal mass under ten centimeters, or a completely resected abdominal lesion. High risk includes stage one with an abdominal mass, an extra-abdominal mass over ten centimeters, or stage two through four disease. For patients under sixty who are low risk, options include CODOX-M with intrathecal chemotherapy, dose-adjusted EPOCH plus rituximab guided by interim PET response, or HyperCVAD alternating with cytarabine and high dose methotrexate plus rituximab. High risk patients, especially those with symptomatic CNS disease, need regimens with strong CNS penetration, such as CODOX-M alternating with IVAC, or HyperCVAD, both with intrathecal therapy, or dose-adjusted EPOCH-R for those who can't tolerate more aggressive approaches. For patients sixty and older, low risk patients get DA-EPOCH plus rituximab guided by PET, while high risk older patients get dose-adjusted EPOCH-R with intensive intrathecal methotrexate for CNS disease.
keypoints: CHOP is NOT adequate therapy for Burkitt lymphoma
Low risk: normal LDH, stage I, small or completely resected mass
High risk: abdominal mass, mass >10cm, or stage II-IV disease
Younger patients: CODOX-M, DA-EPOCH-RR, or HyperCVAD + rituximab
CNS disease requires CNS-penetrating regimens plus intrathecal chemo
keypoint_voiceover: The key testable point is that CHOP is inadequate for Burkitt lymphoma. Risk stratification depends on LDH, stage, and mass size and location. Younger low risk patients get CODOX-M, dose-adjusted EPOCH-RR, or HyperCVAD. High risk or CNS-involved patients need CNS-penetrating regimens with intrathecal chemotherapy built in.
